planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Wintergreen boxwood holds its green winter color better than many boxwood cultivars, which often bronze in cold weather.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Wintergreen boxwood holds its green winter color better than many boxwood cultivars, which often bronze in cold weather. Small, glossy, bright green leaves cover a dense, rounded, exceptionally cold-hardy boxwood selection bred for reliable survival in harsh northern winters where many traditional boxwood cultivars suffer dieback, while retaining fresh green foliage color through the coldest months rather than the bronzing common in less hardy types. Its combination of superior cold hardiness and good winter color has made it a popular substitute for English boxwood in colder climates, used for low hedges, edging, and formal shapes much like its more tender relatives. Shear in late spring or early summer to maintain a formal shape, water during establishment and dry spells, and provide good air circulation to reduce the fungal disease pressure that affects many boxwood plantings.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Prince is a male pollinator cultivar and produces no berries itself but is needed nearby for female Blue Girl or Blue Princess holly to fruit.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Prince is a male pollinator cultivar and produces no berries itself but is needed nearby for female Blue Girl or Blue Princess holly to fruit. Small, spiny, glossy, blue-green leaves cover a dense, compact, exceptionally cold-hardy holly bred by crossing English and evergreen Japanese holly species, holding its rich blue-green color and dense form through harsh winters that damage many other broadleaf evergreen hollies. As the male counterpart in the popular Blue-series holly pairing, it produces no berries of its own but is essential for pollinating nearby female Blue Princess or Blue Girl hollies, which cannot set their showy red berries without a male plant within pollination range. Plant one male for every three to five female Blue-series hollies, shear lightly to maintain shape if a formal hedge is wanted, and provide the same acidic, well-drained soil other hollies prefer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Shamrock inkberry is a compact selection that holds a denser form than the species without the legginess older inkberry cultivars develop.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Shamrock inkberry is a compact selection that holds a denser form than the species without the legginess older inkberry cultivars develop. Small, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves cover a dense, rounded native shrub that serves as a broadleaf evergreen alternative to boxwood, tolerating wetter soil and more shade than boxwood while providing similar year-round structure for a foundation planting or low hedge. Native to wetlands and pinelands of the eastern and southeastern United States, it is more compact and less prone to the bare, leggy lower growth that plagues many older inkberry cultivars, and only female plants produce the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator nearby for fruit set. Shear lightly if a more formal shape is wanted, and provide consistently moist, acidic soil, since inkberry tolerates wetter conditions than most broadleaf evergreens.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Spire euonymus grows in a naturally upright, columnar form requiring minimal shearing to maintain a narrow hedge or screen.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Spire euonymus grows in a naturally upright, columnar form requiring minimal shearing to maintain a narrow hedge or screen. Small, glossy, dark green, evergreen leaves cover a naturally narrow, upright, columnar shrub that provides quick vertical screening or a tidy formal hedge without the wide footprint of rounder evergreen shrubs, tolerating regular shearing and heat well. Fast-growing and adaptable to a range of soils, it is commonly used for narrow foundation plantings, privacy screens along property lines, or formal accents flanking an entrance where a slim, columnar evergreen form is wanted. Shear lightly through the growing season to maintain a tight form, and watch for euonymus scale, a common pest that can build up on stressed or crowded plants.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Texanum ligustrum tolerates heat, humidity, and heavy pruning well, a mainstay hedge shrub across the Gulf South.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Texanum ligustrum tolerates heat, humidity, and heavy pruning well, a mainstay hedge shrub across the Gulf South. Broad, glossy, dark green, wax-textured leaves cover a dense, fast-growing shrub topped in early summer by conspicuous clusters of small white flowers with a strong, sweet scent some find pleasant and others find overpowering, followed by small dark berries that birds readily consume and disperse. A more compact, rounder-leaved selection than the straight species, it has long been one of the most widely planted hedge and screening shrubs across the warm, humid South, tolerating heavy shearing, heat, and drought once established, though it can self-sow aggressively and is considered invasive in some regions. Shear regularly to control size and maintain a formal hedge, and monitor for self-sown seedlings in naturalistic areas, since birds spread the berries widely.
